question: In pinned Liberty NYW case 26-W-0358 filings, Identify the two prospective reporting duties requested in Staff’s discovery letter, compare the Company’s opposition, and follow each duty into the partial ruling. Which duty was directed and which request was denied?
answer: Staff asks to copy the judges on anticipated-delay communications and provide a weekly outstanding-request list on successive Mondays. The Company opposes the separate weekly reporting burden. The ruling directs copying the judges on anticipated-delay communications and denies the remainder, directing the parties first to resolve tracking differences themselves.

evidence.locator: Physical PDF page 2; Discovery request → company response → partial ruling; named original filing and numbered source lines/rows
evidence.quote: Case 26-W-0358 2 responses (i.e., instances where the Company will take more than 10 calendar days to respond to all or a portion of an information request) to the Judges as well as the parties going forward. In addition, we request the Judges require the Company to provide a weekly list on successive Mondays, identifying IRs the Company has received but not yet fully responded to, the status of the responses, when the full response is or was due, and when the Company expects to provide a response, for as long as the Company has outstanding discovery requests in this proceeding. Staff’s requested relief should minimize or eliminate any disputes over timing of responses for Staff and the other parties in this proceeding. We intend to continue working in good faith with the Company and resolve discovery disputes amicably between the parties directly when possible, but we must weigh this against Staff’s reliance upon timely responses to coordinate our review.

evidence.locator: Physical PDF page 3; Discovery request → company response → partial ruling; named original filing and numbered source lines/rows
evidence.quote: However, requiring the Company to prepare a separate weekly report on the status of all outstanding discovery requests is unnecessary and counterproductive. Company personnel already engage in extensive informal communications and meetings with their DPS Staff counterparts on discovery issues. In addition, the Company always includes the information required by the discovery regulations with respect to planned response time if it is unable to provide the response within 10 days, meaning DPS Staff is fully capable of consolidating anticipated response times into a single tracker with its own resources should it desire to manage discovery in that fashion. Most importantly, the reporting requirement proposed by DPS Staff would divert Company personnel from the very task DPS Staff claims to be concerned about: preparing substantive discovery responses. Company resources are better devoted to gathering responsive information, coordinating with appropriate subject-matter experts, and responding to DPS Staff’s requests than to preparing weekly status reports concerning those same requests with information that DPS Staff already has available to it in the form required by the governing discovery regulations. For all of these reasons, the Company respectfully requests that Your Honors deny DPS Staff’s request for the imposition of additional discovery reporting requirements. The Company is complying with the discovery rules, DPS Staff has identified no unresolved discovery dispute requiring intervention, and DPS Staff has demonstrated no prejudice warranting the prospective reporting obligations it seeks.

evidence.quote: To the Parties, On Wednesday, August 26, 2026, Department of Public Service Staff (Staff) filed a mot ion requesting a change in procedure regarding discovery. Staff explained th at, although it has not formally disputed Liberty Utilities (New York Water) Corp.'s (the Company) extensions under 16 NYC RR 5.3 (d) of the 10-d ay period for responding to informat ion requests and eithe r tac itly accepted the extensions or conversed directly with the Compa ny regarding certain delayed responses, the delays and shifting of response times have been increasi ng and now present challe nges to Staff's timely review of the matte r. Staff therefo re requested that we require the Compa ny to (1) provide us wit h copies of emails stating any anticipated delays in its responses (i.e., instances where the Company will take mo re tha n 10 calendar days to respond to all or a portion of an information request) and (2) provide us and th e parties with a weekly list on success ive Mondays, identify ing inform ation requests the Compa ny has received but not yet fully responded to, the status of th e responses, when the full response is or was due, and when the Company expects to provide a response, for as long as th e Company has outstand ing discove ry requests in this proceeding. In response, the Company explains that it has agreed to Staff's request tha t it incl ude in any initial response stating a need for an extension (1 ) a fulsome explanation of the reasons it needs more time and (2) a mo re exact indication of the timing of its substantive response , as well as prompt notice if circums tances require that anticip ated date to be revised. The Company now agrees to copy the Administrat ive Law Judges on those commu nications , which would satisfy Staff's first request. Regarding Staff's seco nd request , the Company notes th at 16 NYC RR 5.9 (c) requires that parties "atte mpt to resolve discovery disputes among themselves, without involvement of th e presidin g officer," and asserts that Staff did not previously raise its proposed reporting requirements with the Company or otherwise attempt to determine whet her the parties could resolve the issue informally before seeking our interventio n. The Company further contends that, of DPS Staff's 335 discovery requests due before the Company filed its response to Staff's motion, only 2 remain outstanding (i.e., 0.6%). In light of the fore going, we gr~nt Staff' s mot ion in part and direct the Company to copy us on its commun icat ions regarding anticipated delays of its responses to discovery requests. However, given the limi ted number of discovery requests that remain outs tanding, we deny the remainde r of Staff' s motion and direct the parties to first attempt to resolve their differences over the track ing of antici pated response times without our involve ment, as required by Rule 5.9 (c). Should good faith attempts to resolve tho se differences fail and th ere are unreso lved discovery disp utes requiring intervention , any party may make another motion request ing changes to discove ry procedures.

question: In pinned Liberty NYW case 26-W-0358 filings, Compare Staff’s 26-of-95 description for responses originally due August 1–24 with the Company’s 69-of-95 preliminary-ten-day description. Give exact calculated percentages rounded to two decimals and explain why the separately quoted 2-of-335 figure is not the same denominator.
answer: 26/95 = 27.37%; 69/95 = 72.63%, complementary framings of the named 95-request initial-due cohort. The Company’s 2/335 = 0.60% describes requests still outstanding by its response date, a larger different cohort/status measure, not the 95-request initial-deadline fraction. These are attributed party claims.

evidence.locator: Physical PDF page 1; Attribution and denominator in discovery counts; named original filing and numbered source lines/rows
evidence.quote: To summarize the issue, the Company has regularly informed Staff that the Company will take more than 10 days to provide responses to certain information requests. Staff has not formally disputed these extensions, either tacitly accepting them or conversing directly with the Company regarding certain delayed responses to try and accommodate both parties’ interests in orderly discovery. However, these delays have increased as discovery has progressed. For responses originally due from August 1 through the 24, the Company has stated it will take more than 10 days to respond to 26 of 95 responses, providing new anticipated response dates in emails sent either shortly before, on, or after the due date of these information requests, with no additional explanation provided in most of these correspondences. On average, these extensions have been for a week. Moreover, the Company has imposed further extensions on the timing of multiple responses, portions of responses, or agreed upon necessary supplements or corrections to its responses in addition to previous extensions, totaling 14 or more days in some instances.

evidence.locator: Physical PDF page 2; Attribution and denominator in discovery counts; named original filing and numbered source lines/rows
evidence.quote: Over the last month, the Company has responded to a striking volume of discovery requests from DPS Staff. From August 4 to August 27, 2026, DPS Staff served 107 discovery requests on the Company (DPS-262 through DPS-368). From August 4 through August 17, DPS Staff served a tranche of discovery requests on the Company every single business day, and almost always at the close of business, which further compresses the practical time available to gather information and prepare responses. Notwithstanding that constant stream of discovery requests, DPS Staff acknowledges that for the 95 requests initially due from August 1 to August 24, the Company provided responsive information/documents within the preliminary 10-day deadline 73% of the time (69 of 95 discovery requests).4 DPS Staff asserts that for the 27% of those discovery requests where the Company needed more than the default 10 days to provide a substantive response (as allowed under 16 NYCRR §§ 5.3 [d] and 5.4 [c]), the Company’s average extension has “been for a week” – with extensions “totaling 14 or more days in some instances.”5 Moreover, of DPS Staff’s 335 discovery requests to the Company due before today, only 2 remain outstanding (i.e., 0.6%).

evidence.quote: To summarize the issue, the Company has regularly informed Staff that the Company will take more than 10 days to provide responses to certain information requests. Staff has not formally disputed these extensions, either tacitly accepting them or conversing directly with the Company regarding certain delayed responses to try and accommodate both parties’ interests in orderly discovery. However, these delays have increased as discovery has progressed. For responses originally due from August 1 through the 24, the Company has stated it will take more than 10 days to respond to 26 of 95 responses, providing new anticipated response dates in emails sent either shortly before, on, or after the due date of these information requests, with no additional explanation provided in most of these correspondences. On average, these extensions have been for a week. Moreover, the Company has imposed further extensions on the timing of multiple responses, portions of responses, or agreed upon necessary supplements or corrections to its responses in addition to previous extensions, totaling 14 or more days in some instances.

evidence.quote: Over the last month, the Company has responded to a striking volume of discovery requests from DPS Staff. From August 4 to August 27, 2026, DPS Staff served 107 discovery requests on the Company (DPS-262 through DPS-368). From August 4 through August 17, DPS Staff served a tranche of discovery requests on the Company every single business day, and almost always at the close of business, which further compresses the practical time available to gather information and prepare responses. Notwithstanding that constant stream of discovery requests, DPS Staff acknowledges that for the 95 requests initially due from August 1 to August 24, the Company provided responsive information/documents within the preliminary 10-day deadline 73% of the time (69 of 95 discovery requests).4 DPS Staff asserts that for the 27% of those discovery requests where the Company needed more than the default 10 days to provide a substantive response (as allowed under 16 NYCRR §§ 5.3 [d] and 5.4 [c]), the Company’s average extension has “been for a week” – with extensions “totaling 14 or more days in some instances.”5 Moreover, of DPS Staff’s 335 discovery requests to the Company due before today, only 2 remain outstanding (i.e., 0.6%). The Company would ideally prefer to provide substantive responses to all DPS Staff’s discovery requests within the initial 10-day window. Unfortunately, however, the sheer number of DPS Staff’s requests (107 discovery requests served in just over three weeks), the overlapping timing of those requests, the complexity and multi-part nature of many of those requests, the voluminous responsive information/documents, and the fact that relevant Company personnel have competing responsibilities related to providing safe and reliable water service, make it impracticable for the Company to always provide the requested information/documents in 10 days – which, again, is expressly contemplated in the discovery rules themselves. 6 In light of the foregoing, it is unremarkable that the Company has needed additional days to provide DPS Staff’s requested information/documents about 27% of the time. Although not required under the discovery rules or even acknowledged in the DPS Staff Letter, the Company recently agreed that if it could not provide DPS Staff’s requested information/documents within the initial 10-day period, the Company would include in its initial response (1) a more fulsome explanation of the reasons it needed more time, (2) a more exact indication of the timing of its substantive response, and (3) prompt notice if circumstances require 3 16 NYCRR §§ 5.3 (c, d), 5.4 (b, c). 4 DPS Staff Letter at 1. 5 Id. It is unclear how DPS Staff calculated a purported one-week average extension. According to the Company’s calculations, the average extension for responses served in August was 4.6 days. 6 See 16 NYCRR §§ 5.3 (d), 5.4 (c).
